From a 2008 national postal survey of 112 SABIO-member beekeepers (22.4% response rate) managing an estimated 19,520 hives at 2,094 apiary sites; figure is self-reported and un-weighted. Table 7 (same doc, p.13-14) shows wide variance by region/operation-focus/size for the same year: e.g. 'All' region, honey-focused, all-size operations = 25.1-26.9 kg/hive/yr across 3 survey sites; Western Cape honey-focused = 23.6-27.9 kg/hive/yr; Western Cape pollination-focused, small operations = only 7.0-7.5 kg/hive/yr. The same document also quotes an earlier, more rigorously validated study: 'Their average reported yield is very low, at just 13.4 kilograms per hive' for Western Cape hives (Allsopp & Cherry 2004, cited p.2 of this working paper), and historical national bee-census data of 8.3 kg/hive/annum (1911-1988 average) rising to 24 kg/hive in the 1974/5 census (same doc, p.1). No single number can be called definitive; 25 kg/hive/yr is used as the document's own headline national estimate.

Every cattle owner must register an official identification mark and brand or mark their cattle with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

No animal may be slaughtered anywhere but a registered abattoir, with the exception below.

Combined data from three extensively-grazed Nguni stud herds, animals born 1968-2015.
Dairy farmers are legally required to test their herds for bovine TB, mainly because of export requirements, so most dairy cattle in South Africa are tested.
Any suspected or confirmed brucellosis-related abortion in cattle must be reported to the State Veterinary office, under the national bovine brucellosis control scheme.
A cull cow may be slaughtered only at an abattoir, except for the farmer's own consumption or for cultural or religious purposes.

In hotter, humid KZN, KZN DARD describes Nguni × Jersey dairy trials at Makhathini to combine milk potential with local adaptation. Hand milking with the calf present highlights competition between household milk and calf growth. Discuss adapted stock and feeding locally; commercial milk-recording totals do not forecast this system. Record calving, lactation stage and milk available after calf needs.

Table 1, AFC column, rows in the table's order Holstein-Friesland Reg./Grade, Jersey Reg./Grade, Ayrshire Reg./Grade: 28, 30, 25, 28, 29, 32 months. The Grade rows used here are Holstein-Friesland 30 and Jersey 28 (Grade Ayrshire 32 is not used: the enterprise is Jersey or Holstein type). 28 x 4.35 = 121.8 weeks; 30 x 4.35 = 130.5 weeks. Milk begins at first calving, so age at first calving is the time to first product.

Table 1 ('Comparison of number of cows, production and fertility in the main dairy breeds in South Africa'), Milk column, Grade rows: Jersey 3840 kg and Holstein-Friesland 5422 kg per lactation (Registered rows: 4468 and 6426 kg). The document says these are National Milk Recording Scheme herds, which 'have been shown to be better managed than those outside the scheme, with their performance per lactation being 50 % greater than that of the national herd', so a smallholder herd should expect less.
Holstein 739.33 and Jersey 696.81 days of productive life (first calving to culling) in South African milk-recorded herds, 2000-2019: 696.81/365.25 = 1.91 and 739.33/365.25 = 2.02 years.
Commercial dairy processors require an even year-round milk supply. This is a herd supply reference, not year-round milk from each cow. Confirm your farm's calving and milking months.
An owner or manager whose animals are, or may be, infected with a controlled animal disease must report it to the state veterinary director immediately.
Newcastle disease and notifiable avian influenza are on the state list of controlled and notifiable animal diseases.
No animal may be slaughtered anywhere but an abattoir, with the exceptions below.
Slaughter for your own household, or for cultural or religious purposes, is exempt from the abattoir rule.

Newer South African commercial reference: SAPA 2024 reports average slaughter at 30–31 days with bird weight 1.8–1.85 kg. The primary range above remains the earlier 2022 reference at 32–33 days. These are commercial bird weights, not dressed meat kg or a village flock target. Record hatch or purchase age, feeding system, actual harvest date and weighed product basis.

32 days / 7 = 4.57 weeks; 33 days / 7 = 4.71 weeks. This enterprise has a single grow-out cycle ending in slaughter, so 'time to first product' = age at slaughter. South Africa, commercial industry average.

National commercial broiler industry average, South Africa, 2022. A separate breed-trial table (Table 4b, same document, p.39) gives named-strain 'Cumulative FI (kg)' and 'Body weight (kg)' at exactly 35 days: Arbor Acres Plus 2.29kg, Cobb 500 2.52kg, Indian River 2.30kg, Ross 308 2.30kg (cumulative feed intake 3.21-3.64kg) - a slightly older age (35 vs 32-33 days) and higher weight than the industry-wide average quoted above; not merged into the primary figure since it is a different (breed-standard trial) dataset, but used below for the feed-intake figure.

The ARC Irene trial compared Potchefstroom Koekoek, Venda, Ovambo and Naked Neck under commercial feed, water and controlled lighting. Mean eggs/hen in a 52-week cycle were 195.9, 153.7, 125.5 and 138.9 respectively; first-egg ages were 138.5, 139.0, 134.5 and 129.0 days from hatch, with no significant first-egg age difference among breeds. This is managed breed context, not the yield of scavenging hens in KZN. Match feeding and housing before using a benchmark.

Free-range village chickens, KwaZulu-Natal; dry-environment birds started laying earlier (15.74 weeks) than wet-environment birds (27.78 weeks), difference flagged significant ('*') in the source table. Wide range reflects genuine dry/wet-season environmental variation reported by the source, not measurement uncertainty.

Free-range/scavenging village chickens, KwaZulu-Natal: dry (40.43) vs wet (49.91) environment, difference not significant ('NS'). A managed-system ARC Irene trial of named indigenous breeds (Grobbelaar, Sutherland & Molalakgotla 2010, Animal Genetic Resources 46: 25-32) reports far higher counts, now separately verified and retained in productionReferences; managed conditions cannot replace this village range.

SAPA 2024 commercial strain standards cumulative to 90 weeks: Dekalb Amberlink 429 eggs/hen housed, Dekalb Brown 428, Hy-Line Silver Brown 435, Hy-Line Brown 434 and Lohmann Brown Lite 413. These are full-cycle objectives, not eggs per calendar year or a smallholder forecast. Purchase age, actual onset of lay, surviving laying hens, feed, water and lighting need separate records.

Commercial layer reference: bird age from hatch, not weeks after buying point-of-lay pullets or building housing. Supplier strain, rearing and actual onset can differ. The former 16–17 week figure was the SAPA receiving/housing age, not evidence of first eggs.

Table 4a's cumulative 'Eggs/hen housed' for five commercial strains; the same table gives 'Age at depop. weeks 90.0' for every strain. Commercial barn/cage average, not a free-range smallholder trial. Kept as the source gives it: a per-year rate would need a point-of-lay age from another document.
With a constant 14–16 hour light day, commercial hens keep laying at a high rate all year.
Ducks are one of the domesticated animal species listed in the Meat Safety Act, so its rules on registered abattoirs and hygiene apply to them.
Ducks slaughtered to be sold must be slaughtered at a registered abattoir; slaughter for the farmer's own consumption is exempt but that meat may not be sold.
At the abattoir, ducks must be handled humanely during loading, transport, offloading, housing, immobilising and killing, under the Animals Protection Act.
Ducks are birds/poultry, so an outbreak of avian influenza in a duck flock is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act and must be reported to the state vet immediately.

P44 = Pekin (7 weeks to slaughter); MR71 = Muscovy (10 weeks for ducks/hens, 12 weeks for drakes). Treated as 'time to first product' = age to slaughter, since this is a single-cycle meat enterprise (no repeat product like eggs). Non-South-African trial by Warsaw researchers, published in SAJAS; journal location does not establish local applicability.

Non-SA (Guyana study reporting a citation to Steklenev 1990); no SA-specific absolute slaughter live-weight figure was found (see gaps). 2.93 kg = Pekin at 8-10 weeks, 2.29 kg = Muscovy at 8-10 weeks - matches this enterprise's two breeds. The same LRRD paper's own experiment (Table 2, intensive system, Guyana) measured live weight at slaughter (8 weeks) as: Pekin drakes 2.53 kg, Pekin hens 2.29 kg, Muscovy drakes 2.47 kg, Muscovy hens 1.51 kg - broadly consistent with, but not merged into, the cited range above since it is a separate dataset/table in the same source. No sourced eggs/duck/year figure was found for either breed (see gaps); the LRRD and SAJAS sources used here studied ducks reared only for meat.
The indigenous Mozambique Tilapia (O. mossambicus) is not a listed invasive species and may be farmed without an alien-species permit; the faster-growing Nile Tilapia (O. niloticus) is.

Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) is a nationally listed invasive fish species: Category 1b inside National Parks, Provincial Reserves, Mountain Catchment Areas and Forestry Reserves, and Category 3 in all other areas.
Outside protected areas Nile tilapia is Category 3: it may remain in prescribed areas or provinces, but further propagation or trade is prohibited.
Nile Tilapia has been listed under the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Regulations as requiring a permit to produce.
Producing an alien or invasive species (such as Nile Tilapia) is prohibited in areas designated under the Protected Areas Act and the Fish Sanctuary Act; a permit is required to produce it elsewhere.
Producing tilapia in South Africa requires a water use licence under the National Water Act.

ARC makes tilapia suitability depend on water temperature: summer grow-out can be suitable anywhere in South Africa when water exceeds 20°C; growth is poor below 18°C and winter water below 13°C can kill farmed tilapia. The Highveld reference is a summer crop; tunnels can widen the range. Measure pond water and confirm stocking species and dates. Air climate or a mapped pond does not prove harvest months, fish numbers or food kg.

10 months x 4.35 = 43.5 weeks; 12 months x 4.35 = 52.2 weeks. This is Mozambique Tilapia (O. mossambicus) grow-out time to harvestable size; the source separately states Nile Tilapia (O. niloticus) reaches harvestable maturity faster, in 6-10 months (= 26.1-43.5 weeks) — not used here as it is a different species with a different legal status (see 'legal').

Table 8-3 gives the Mozambique Tilapia's harvestable size as an approximate single figure ('+- 800g'), not a range, so [800, 800] is used rather than inventing a spread. The same table cell wraps '10-12' across a line break in the PDF ('10-\n12'), kept verbatim. The table's Nile Tilapia row gives the same approximate weight (+-800g) reached faster, in 6-10 months — not used here because this dossier is framed around the indigenous, legally unrestricted Mozambique Tilapia per task instruction; see 'legal' for why Nile Tilapia is treated separately. No SA source was found giving a feed-conversion-based or per-hectare yield figure specific to O. mossambicus that could be converted to this per-fish unit without stitching numbers across documents, so outputUnit follows the source's own unit (grams harvest weight per fish) rather than being converted.
Winter water temperatures halt tilapia growth over most of South Africa; only the sub-tropical North-East supports year-round unheated grow-out.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act: veterinary services enforce isolation and movement restrictions, and a suspected case must be reported.

Inside a declared FMD-affected zone, goats and their products (including milk) cannot be moved into, out of, or within the zone without a state veterinary movement permit and compliance with its conditions.
Every goat owner must register an official identification mark and mark their goats with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

A goat may only be slaughtered for sale at a registered abattoir under the Meat Safety Act (relevant when culled dairy does or male kids are sold for meat); slaughtering for the farmer's own consumption, or for cultural/religious purposes, is exempt but that meat may not then be sold.

South African Saanen reference by lactation number, not age in years: mean milk mass per standardised 305-day lactation was 947.3 kg at first parity, 1043.2 at second, 1073.4 at third, 1020.3 at fourth, 972.8 at fifth, 901.6 at sixth and 775.4 at ≥7th. These ARC milk-recorded groups were mostly intensive/semi-intensive stud herds. Record actual kidding date, lactation number and collected milk; do not divide these totals evenly into months.

At Putukwane near Polokwane, 179 lactating does under extensive feeding with irregular supplementation were observed for 210 days after kidding. Mean milk mass was 1.45 kg/day for Saanen, 0.75 for British Alpine and 0.56 for Toggenburg during observed lactation. Early lactation exceeded mid and late lactation; March–April kidding outperformed October–November in this cohort. These conditions differ from stud-herd records. Discuss adapted stock and feed locally; these are not litres/day or year-round promises.

Lowest (≥7th parity) and highest (3rd parity) group means for milk yield per 305-day standardised lactation in 16,407 analysed South African ARC Saanen lactation records, 1955–2018, mostly intensive/semi-intensive stud herds. Original PDF Table 3 labels the last group ≥7th; HTML renders it >7th. Kept in kg, without litres conversion, annualisation or yield-by-age interpolation.

In this South African Saanen milk-recording study, does kidding in spring had the highest average lactation milk yield. Table 1 defines spring as August–October for this study. These are kidding-season categories, not confirmed milk collection months.
Inside a declared FMD-affected zone, goats and their products cannot be moved into, out of, or within the zone without a state veterinary movement permit and compliance with its conditions.
Every goat owner, including communal/smallholder owners, must register an official identification mark and mark their goats with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

A goat may only be slaughtered for sale at a registered abattoir under the Meat Safety Act; slaughtering it for the farmer's own consumption, or for cultural/religious purposes (including ceremonial slaughter, common with indigenous goats), is exempt from that rule, but that meat may not then be sold.

The 2016 government goat manual distinguishes indigenous, Boer, Savanna and Kalahari Red meat-purpose stock from milk/fibre breeds, with breeding objectives and individual birth, weaning, weight and sale records. Uncontrolled communal mating can produce births at any time; that does not establish meat or weaned-kid availability all year. Choose stock for the local system and record survival and product stage before forecasting quantities.

In KZN Highland Sourveld smallholder systems, winter and early-spring feed shortage can restrict goats. Autumn-kidding does feed kids through winter; spring-kidding does face late-pregnancy feed shortage, especially with late rains. Plan local winter feed and monitor weights with extension support; this is regional care context, not kg or a universal kidding calendar.

This is age at first KIDDING (birth of first kids), not first weaned kids. 16 months x 4.35 = 69.6 weeks; 18 months x 4.35 = 78.3 weeks, from doe birth to her giving birth for the first time. Adding the source's own ~150-day (~5-month, ~21.75-week) weaning assumption would put first WEANED kids at roughly 91-100 weeks of doe age, but that compound figure is not shown as the primary value since the field is documented as 'age/time from start (hatch, birth) to first product' and first kidding is the clearer, directly-stated milestone; the weaning offset is noted here for transparency.
Breeding is not controlled and happens all year, but in one Mpumalanga communal study kidding rates were highest in autumn (96%) and spring (93%), lower in winter (63%) and nil in summer.

A goat may only be slaughtered for sale at a registered abattoir under the Meat Safety Act; slaughtering it for the farmer's own consumption, or for cultural/religious purposes, is exempt from that rule, but that meat may not then be sold.

The reported weaning rate is 149%, or 1.49 kids weaned per doe mated. The source describes observations over twenty years for extensive Boer does at 295 mm rainfall; it does not state kids weaned per doe per calendar year. This is a reproductive outcome, not kg of live animals or dressed meat. A separate mean litter size of 1.93 kids born per parturition has a different denominator and stage and is not merged into this figure.

Breeding/kidding is not confined to one season - Boer does kid throughout the year - but kidding is concentrated in three peaks: March-April, June-July and September-October, with an overall peak in autumn.
African swine fever (ASF) is listed as a controlled animal disease pertaining to pigs under the Animal Diseases Act; warthogs and Ornithodorus ticks are carriers/vectors.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is also listed as a controlled animal disease pertaining to pigs under the Animal Diseases Act.
Swill (food waste) may not be fed to pigs unless it has been boiled for at least 60 minutes or sterilised by another equally effective method.
Pigs may only be moved into a biosecure compartment from another compartment that is officially certified/approved for that purpose.
A pig may not be slaughtered anywhere but a registered abattoir, except for own household consumption or cultural/religious purposes.
A pig owner must apply to register an official identification mark and mark their pigs with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

ARC Table 1 lists pregnant sows at 10–18 L drinking water/day and lactating sows at 18–23 L/day. These are breeding-sow stages, not one amount for every pig. Farrowing care separates sow cooling from piglet warmth; outdoor systems need locally adapted hardy stock, shade and shelter. Confirm stage, reliable clean water, feed and housing locally. The manual supplies no verified edible kg per breeding sow for this plan.
Rabbits are one of the domesticated animal species listed in the Meat Safety Act, so the Act's rules on abattoirs and hygiene apply to them, as they do to ducks and other listed species.
Rabbits slaughtered to be sold must be slaughtered at a registered abattoir; slaughter for the farmer's own consumption is exempt from this rule but the meat from it may not be sold.
At the abattoir, rabbits (like other listed animals) must be handled humanely during loading, transport, offloading, housing, immobilising and killing, under the Animals Protection Act.

The wild European rabbit (the same species as farmed New Zealand White/Californian rabbits) is only listed as an invasive species under NEMBA on South Africa's off-shore islands - it is not a listed/restricted species on the mainland.

South African grower reference: New Zealand White and Phendula rabbits in the 2017 Stellenbosch trial were slaughtered at about 11 weeks from birth. Overall means were 2.62 kg live slaughter weight, 1.55 kg hot carcass, 1.48 kg chilled carcass and 1.26 kg reference carcass with head and red offal removed, still including bones. Balanced pellets and water were freely available in a grower house. These weights are not boneless meat or annual doe output; do not multiply them by the unrelated FAO backyard target.

FAO general backyard target, not a South African observed rate. The 30–35 young per doe annually have reached slaughter or reproduction age after allowance for post-weaning loss; they are not merely weaned and are not kg of meat. The source models six litters and 5.5 surviving young per litter, describing a 30-rabbit objective; an extra litter raises its stated objective to 35. Do not combine this backyard target with grower-house carcass weight from a different trial.

279 days / 365 = 0.76 years. This figure is from French INTENSIVE commercial rabbitries (average of 1992 national recording-scheme data), NOT backyard/extensive hutches - the source gives no separate productive-life figure for backyard systems (see gaps). Treat as a lower-bound / industrial-system reference only.
In hot, humid wet-season conditions rabbit reproduction rates fall; artificial lighting in managed hutches can largely offset this.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act; Veterinary Services enforce isolation and movement restrictions.
Inside a declared FMD zone, sheep and their products cannot be moved into, out of, or within it without a state veterinary permit.
Sheep scab is a controlled disease by law: a suspected or positive case must be reported to the State Veterinarian immediately.
Against sheep scab, all small stock on the farm must be treated with a remedy registered under Act 36 of 1947, and infected sheep treated twice, eight to ten days apart.
Every sheep owner must register an official identification mark and mark their sheep with it, under the Animal Identification Act.
A sheep may be slaughtered only at an abattoir, except for the farmer's own consumption or for cultural or religious purposes.

The government sheep manual describes controlled breeding at Mara Research Station, Limpopo: June–July mating and November–December lambing to match rain and grass. This is one station breeding calendar, not mutton harvest months. Match adapted meat-purpose stock and feed locally, then record birth, survival, weaning and actual slaughter or sale; lambs born per ewe are not edible kg.

outputUnit is 'lambs born/ewe/year' rather than the suggested 'kg live weight/lamb at weaning or slaughter' or 'lambs weaned/ewe/year': the source explains 'Measuring accurate lambing percentages for smallholder sheep farmers is challenging as these farmers mostly farm extensively and do not keep records', and instead calculates 'Lambs born per ewe (as recorded from the surveys based on interviews with individual respondents)' - a lambing (born), not weaning, figure, self-reported by smallholder farmers rather than measured/weighed. 139%=1.39, 83%=0.83, 61%=0.61 lambs born/ewe/year; the range [0.61, 1.39] spans the three Western Cape smallholder districts surveyed (Eden, Central Karoo, West Coast), all from this one study/quote - not merged with any other document. The same paper separately states a COMMERCIAL extensive benchmark of 110-156% lambing and 94-132% weaning (Snyman & Herselman, 2005), explicitly 'expressed over ewes joined' (a different denominator/system) - not merged into this smallholder range.
Despite foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) in South Africa, wool exports continue under the inactivation clause of the OIE (World Organisation for Animal Health) rules.
Wool from scab-infected sheep must be destroyed rather than sent to the buyer, where it would be marked as scab wool.

Semi-arid/extensive-veld range (4-5 kg greasy wool/sheep/year) used as the primary value; the same sentence's 8 kg/year figure is for a different system (sheep grazing CULTIVATED pastures) and is deliberately excluded from the range rather than averaged in. A Western Cape Government (Elsenburg) Dohne Merino Extensive enterprise budget (Ceres-Karoo, 2024) separately reports total flock wool sold as 4439.64 kg from a flock of '1 519' Smallstock Units, i.e. 4439.64/1519 = 2.92 kg per Smallstock Unit/year - not used as the primary value because the source does not state that 1 Smallstock Unit = 1 sheep (SSU is a standardised stock-class weighting, not a literal head count), so converting it to kg/sheep would require an unstated conversion factor. A separate NWGA/Mandela Initiative paper on the Eastern Cape communal Wool Sheep Development Program reports a Grootfontein ADI progeny-test 'Greasy fleece weight (kg) 2.8 [commercial rams] 2.4 [communal rams]' for communal Eastern Cape flocks - not merged into the primary value because that table is explicitly for '6-month old lambs' (a different life stage from a mature sheep's full annual clip), consistent with the rule against mixing figures across life stages; kept here only as EC-communal context: commercial-ram-sired lambs at 6 months averaged 2.8 kg, communal-ram-sired lambs 2.4 kg, a +16% difference.
Nationally sheep are shorn from around end-July to mid-May (aggregate across sheds); many farms now shear every 6-8 months rather than once a year.
